races.long_description: Representative Barry Moore, a third-term Republican and longtime Trump loyalist, is running for the Senate seat being vacated by Tommy Tuberville, who is running for governor. Mr. Moore’s Democratic opponent, Everett Wess, a former judge and lawyer, is a long shot in deep-red Alabama.

Senator Dan S. Sullivan, a Republican, is trying to hold on to his seat against former Representative Mary Peltola, a Democrat. The wild card in the four-person ranked-choice race is the presence of Daniel J. Sullivan, a retiree in a small fishing village who has the same name as the incumbent.
Senator Tom Cotton, a Trump ally and the third-ranking Republican in the chamber, is heavily favored to win a third term. He is facing Hallie Shoffner, a Democrat and sixth-generation farmer.

Senator John Hickenlooper, a moderate incumbent, is running for a second term in a solidly Democratic seat. He faces Mark Baisley, a Republican state senator, and Bob Chew, a Navy veteran and former Republican who is running as an independent.

Senator Chris Coons, a Democrat, is heavily favored to win re-election in a state that Kamala Harris carried by about 15 percentage points two years ago. His Republican challenger is Mike Katz, a doctor who has served in Delaware’s State Senate.

Senator Ashley Moody, the Republican incumbent, is on the Senate ballot for the first time, having been appointed last year to finish Marco Rubio’s term. She faces State Representative Angie Nixon, a progressive who won the Democratic primary in an upset.

Senator Jon Ossoff, a Democrat, is seeking a second term in Georgia, a battleground that both parties this cycle initially considered the toughest for Democrats to hold onto. He is facing Representative Mike Collins, a Republican who won President Trump’s endorsement in the primary.

Senator Jim Risch, 83, a Republican, is heavily favored to win a fourth term in Idaho, a state President Trump carried by more than 36 percentage points in 2024. His toughest challenge comes from Todd Achilles, one of several independents challenging Republicans across the country this year.

Illinois’ open Senate seat, now held by retiring Senator Dick Durbin, a Democrat, is likely to remain blue. Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton, a progressive, is favored to prevail over her Republican opponent, Don Tracy, a former chairman of the state Republican Party.

Representative Ashley Hinson, a Republican, is vying to maintain party control of the seat held by retiring Senator Joni Ernst. Polls have shown her locked in a tight race against Josh Turek, a Democratic state representative, in a state that President Trump won three times.

Senator Roger Marshall, a first-term Republican, is trying to survive an unexpectedly competitive race in deep-red Kansas. He faces Adam Hamilton, a centrist Democrat who has sought to corral farmers’ anger at economic conditions under President Trump.

Representative Andy Barr, a Republican, is running to succeed the retiring Senator Mitch McConnell, whose poor health came under scrutiny in recent months. Mr. Barr faces Charles Booker, a progressive former state lawmaker who has run for the Senate twice before.

Senator Bill Cassidy lost his Republican primary this year after President Trump targeted him for voting to convict him in his second impeachment trial. Now the seat Mr. Cassidy held for over a decade is up for grabs, and Representative Julia Letlow, who is backed by Mr. Trump, is heavily favored to win it over Jamie Davis, a Democratic farmer.
Senator Susan Collins, a Republican, is seeking a sixth term against the Democrat Troy Jackson in the toughest political environment she has faced over her 30-year career.

Senator Ed Markey, 80, a Democrat whose progressive bona fides helped him turn back a much younger challenger in the primary, is running for re-election in a solidly Democratic state. He faces John Deaton, a Republican lawyer and a Marine veteran.

Abdul El-Sayed, a Democratic former public health official, is in a competitive race against former Representative Mike Rogers, a Republican who narrowly lost his Senate bid in 2024. The contest has become a key test for progressives, who are backing El-Sayed.

The race to replace the retiring Senator Tina Smith, a Democrat, pits the state’s lieutenant governor, Peggy Flanagan, a Democrat, against Michele Tafoya, a sports journalist and a first-time candidate. The two have sparred over fraud in statewide programs and rising costs attributed to the Iran war and the Trump administration’s tariff policies.

Scott Colom, a Democratic prosecutor, has mounted an unexpectedly competitive challenge to Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, a first-term Republican who has been reliably aligned with President Trump. While Ms. Hyde-Smith is still favored in conservative Mississippi, Mr. Colom would be the first Black senator elected from the state since Reconstruction.

A late withdrawal by the incumbent Republican, Steve Daines, left a Senate seat open in a historically conservative state. Kurt Alme, a Republican backed by President Trump, faces an unusually fractured field after national Democrats and state leaders shifted support toward an independent candidate, Seth Bodnar, instead of the Democrat who won the party’s primary, Alani Bankhead.

Dan Osborn, a mechanic, former union leader and military veteran running as an independent, is challenging Senator Pete Ricketts, a Republican scion of an influential billionaire family with deep ties to Nebraska. To clear the way for Mr. Osborn’s bid, the Democratic primary winner, Cindy Burbank, declined the party’s nomination, potentially consolidating the anti-incumbent vote in the conservative stronghold.

Nearly 20 years ago, John E. Sununu, a Republican, lost his Senate seat to Jeanne Shaheen, a Democrat. Now she is retiring, and Mr. Sununu is trying to make a comeback. He is facing Representative Chris Pappas, a low-key Democrat in his fourth term.
Senator Cory Booker, a Democrat and former Newark mayor elected to the Senate in 2013, faces Justin Murphy, a Republican attorney.

Senator Ben Ray Luján, a Democrat, is running for a second term in a solidly blue state against Larry E. Marker, a former oil and gas producer who won the Republican nomination as a write-in candidate.

Roy Cooper, the Democratic former North Carolina governor, and Michael Whatley, the former Republican National Committee chairman, are competing to succeed Senator Thom Tillis, a Republican who is retiring.

In one of the most expensive and consequential Senate races of this cycle, Senator Jon Husted, a Republican, is facing a challenge from Sherrod Brown, a Democrat. Mr. Brown lost his seat in 2024 after three terms in the Senate.

Markwayne Mullin left the Senate to become secretary of the Department of Homeland Security, and his replacement, Alan Armstrong, is ineligible to seek a full term under state law. Representative Kevin Hern, a Trump ally, is the clear favorite to win the open seat.
Senator Jeff Merkley is running for re-election in a solidly Democratic state. Among his challengers are State Senator David Brock Smith, a Republican, and Gary Lyndon Dye, a Libertarian.

Senator Jack Reed, a Democrat, is seeking a sixth term in a state that has not sent a Republican to the Senate since 2000. He is being challenged by Raymond McKay, a Republican activist who was formerly the network and telecommunications manager for the city of Warwick, R.I.

Senator Darline Graham, the Republican appointed to fill her deceased brother Lindsey Graham’s seat, is running for a full term of her own. Dr. Annie Andrews, a Democrat and a pediatrician, is hoping Ms. Graham’s inexperience and her ties to President Trump can help her flip a seat in a state that hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1998.

Senator Mike Rounds, a Republican, is running for a third term in one of the country’s most conservative states. Public polling has been limited, but some surveys have shown him in a closer-than-usual race with Brian Bengs, an independent. The Democratic nominee withdrew from the ballot.

Senator Bill Hagerty, a Trump-backed Republican, is seeking a second term in a state that President Trump won by nearly 30 points in 2024. His opponent, the Democratic environmental justice activist Marquita Bradshaw, previously ran for Senate in 2020 and 2024.

James Talarico, a state legislator, is trying to become the first Democrat in more than three decades to win a statewide election in Texas. He is facing Ken Paxton, the Republican state attorney general, in a race that is one of the most expensive American campaigns ever.
Senator Mark Warner, a Democrat, is seeking a fourth term in a state that is considered solidly blue. He faces Bert Mizusawa, a retired general who easily won the Republican primary.
Senator Shelley Moore Capito is running for a third term in West Virginia, a Republican stronghold. She faces Rachel Fetty Anderson, a lawyer and a Democratic former city councilwoman in Morgantown.

In deep-red Wyoming, the state’s lone at-large House member, Harriet Hageman, is favored to succeed Senator Cynthia Lummis, a Republican, who is retiring after serving one term. Ms. Hageman faces James Byrd, a Democratic former state lawmaker.

Most voters tend to vote early in person, and vote reporting is usually relatively fast. But if a race is very close, it can still take awhile to declare a winner. In 2022, it took until Wednesday afternoon for The A.P. to declare that the top Senate candidates had advanced to a runoff, which was held on Dec. 6.
In 2022 and 2024, about half of the state’s votes were reported by midnight Eastern time on election night, and the count reached 95 percent around 6 a.m. on Wednesday.

In 2024, just under half of voters cast ballots by mail, and it took about two days to report 95 percent of votes statewide. Postmarked ballots must arrive by the fourth day after the election, Nov. 7.

The state has long conducted its elections by mail. In 2022 and in 2024, it took about four days to report 95 percent of votes in statewide races. If a race is close, it could take awhile for The A.P. to call a winner.

content.text: Susan Collins took the stage at her election-night headquarters in Bangor after the polls closed in Maine to thank her supporters as a crowd of hundreds cheered her on. “We went all over the state and I’ve got to tell you, the crowds were huge, the reception was warm and the response could not have been better,” the Republican incumbent said as she was surrounded by her extended family.
But she noted that it was very early in the night. “The results are going to take a while and we will keep watching,” she said before heading back to her personal watch party.

Roy Cooper’s Senate victory for Democrats in North Carolina has been expected for many weeks now. But it was not a given as the midterm elections were shaping up last year and earlier this year, when North Carolina looked like it might wage one of the most expensive Senate contests of the midterms.
Cooper’s
name recognition and popularity as a former governor
, as well as his succinct campaign slogan, “Make Stuff Cost Less,” helped Democrats shore up North Carolina and free money for the party to compete in other tight states.

How well is the night going for Democrats so far? Democratic candidates for Senate have been declared winners in New Hampshire and North Carolina already, while the race in Kentucky has yet to be called for the Republican nominee.
James Talarico has won the early vote by a wide margin in
Texas

, where only about a quarter of the vote is expected to be cast on Election Day. In the state’s major metropolitan counties, he’s outrunning Kamala Harris by by around 25 percentage points. Ken Paxton will need to win the Election Day vote by a wide margin.

The tightest of Florida House races right now is a tossup between Representative María Elvira Salazar, the incumbent Republican, and Eliott Rodriguez, her Democratic challenger, in a Miami-based district that had been seen as an indicator for potential Hispanic voter backlash over the Trump administration’s aggressive immigration enforcement.

When Republicans have done well in Florida in recent election cycles, it has not necessarily meant that Republicans have done well nationally. But even Gov. Ron DeSantis, a Republican, has said in recent days that an underperformance by the party in his state would probably signal trouble for the G.O.P. in other parts of the country.

At least three Florida Republicans are fighting for their political lives right now in districts that were seen to slightly favor them: Representatives Aaron Bean, Maria Elvira Salazar and Anna Paulina Luna are all within uncomfortably close margins with their Democratic challengers.

At one point in the cycle, the New Hampshire Senate race seemed as if it would be close. But nothing about the completed results in the state thus far suggests an edge for John Sununu, the former Republican senator. In almost all of the municipalities that have finished counting votes, Chris Pappas, the Democratic nominee, is running ahead of Kamala Harris’s margins in 2024, when she won the state by three percentage points.

In the Florida Senate race, the state’s three Hispanic-majority counties are all shifting drastically to the left, providing some early insights into a demographic that will be closely watched nationwide.

President Trump swept Miami-Dade, Hendry and Osceola counties in 2024. But this year, each swung toward Angie Nixon, the Democratic nominee, by at least 18 percentage points. That was enough to flip both Miami-Dade and Osceola, while Ashley Moody, the Republican nominee, held on to Hendry County despite a nearly 27-point swing to the left.
Despite the shifts, our election forecast is still leaning heavily toward Moody.

Senator Darline Graham, the South Carolina Republican appointed to fill her late brother Lindsey’s seat, is running behind the state’s Republican candidate for governor, Alan Wilson, who was heavily favored in his race.

In the Georgia Senate race, Jon Ossoff was quickly declared the winner. He outperformed Kamala Harris’s 2024 margins by an average of 12 percentage points in counties that have mostly finished reporting, and he also did substantially better than his own 2020 margins in many of these counties. That year, the Senate race
went to a runoff
, where he
narrowly defeated
his Republican opponent.

Representative Kathy Castor’s win in Florida is the second for Democrats in a district that Republican state lawmakers redrew in their favor this year. Out of the four districts, Democrats have, for now, held on to two.

Polls have closed in Tennessee, where Republicans are hoping to win all nine congressional seats after redrawing their map this year in response to the Supreme Court ruling that weakened the Voting Rights Act. At a watch party for Senator Marsha Blackburn, who is hoping to become the state’s first female governor and third consecutive Republican, the conservative commentator Clay Travis just declared, “We’re going to have a lot to celebrate.”
Tennessee Governor Election Results ›

The Democrats appear poised for a strong showing, based on the results in more than 100 counties and townships that have completed their vote so far. The party’s candidates are outrunning Kamala Harris’s 2024 performance by a wide margin essentially everywhere reporting so far. If the pattern holds across the country, Democrats would win the national vote by around 10 percentage points.

Representative Kathy Castor, a 10-term Florida Democrat, will keep her seat after defeating Mike Beltran, a Republican former state representative, according to The Associated Press, in a Tampa-area district that the state’s Republicans redrew to heavily favor them.

Castor has been in the House since 2007 and had never truly faced a competitive election, winning each previous race by at least 15 percentage points. She decided to run for an 11th term even after the new map put her in a district, the 14th, which President Trump would have won by more than 10 percentage points had it covered the same territory in 2024.
Florida 14th Congressional District Election Results ›

Representative Jared Moskowitz’s victory for Democrats in Florida’s 25th Congressional District is in one of four districts that Republican state lawmakers redrew this year to benefit their party. Moskowitz decided to run anyway in the Republican-leaning seat, relying on his strong name recognition and deep knowledge of the region to win over new voters.
Florida 25th Congressional District Election Results ›

Georgia was always expected to be a state where a significant number of voters might split their tickets between the Senate and governor’s races, and the results so far suggest that expectation is holding true. Senator Jon Ossoff, a Democrat, has won re-election, defeating his Republican challenger, Representative Mike Collins, while former Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms of Atlanta, a Democrat, holds a narrower lead over Rick Jackson, a Republican, in the governor’s race.

The disparity suggests that some voters who backed Ossoff were less willing to support his fellow Democrat for governor. It also underscores Ossoff’s political strength in a battleground state, where his early victory could outpace support for his party more broadly.

Representative Jared Moskowitz, a centrist Democrat, will remain in Congress after defeating Scott Singer, a Republican, in a South Florida congressional district that had been redrawn by the state’s Republicans to favor their party, according to The Associated Press.

Moskowitz, one of the most prominent Jewish Democrats in Congress, chose to run in Florida’s 25th Congressional District, which stretches along the Atlantic coastline from Miami-Dade to Palm Beach Counties, after Republicans eliminated his former district.
Florida 25th Congressional District Election Results ›

There is no race where more is on the line for Elon Musk than the Senate election in Texas, where most polls just closed. Musk spent over $200 million to try to elect Ken Paxton, a Republican, to the Senate in his home state. Musk has laid out nearly $500 million during the midterms overall, the second-biggest expenditure by a donor even in a campaign cycle. The Texas result is a big test not just of Musk’s influence, but whether enormous political spending truly makes a difference.

Juliana Stratton, the Democratic lieutenant governor of Illinois, defeated Don Tracy, a former state Republican Party chairman, in the state’s Senate race, according to The Associated Press. Stratton’s victory means that next year, three Black women will serve in the Senate at the same time — a first in the institution’s history.
When she takes office, she will serve alongside Senator Tammy Duckworth, a Thai American, making Illinois the first state represented by two women of color in the Senate at the same time.

Polls have closed in Texas, except for El Paso, which is one hour behind. Early vote results will come in first, but several counties will not release even those counts until every person in line has voted.

Kansas, where polls closed at 8 p.m. Eastern, has been reliably red in federal races, but the state has moved leftward in recent years and has had a Democratic governor since 2019. The Senate race between Roger Marshall, the Republican incumbent, and Adam Hamilton, his Democratic challenger, will hinge on counties Democrats have carried in presidential races, as well as areas that supported the re-election of Gov. Laura Kelly, a Democrat, in 2022 and voted for President Trump two years later.
Johnson County

, a suburb of Kansas City where Hamilton lives, will account for over a quarter of the vote. Democrats won Johnson by over eight percentage points in the 2020 and 2024 presidential elections, but Hamilton is looking to make even more inroads there. In the 2022 governor’s race, Kelly won it by 20 points.
Sedgwick County
, which contains Wichita, is a key bellwether and a target for both candidates: Kelly won the county by three points, while Trump won it by more than 13 in 2024.
Shawnee County

, which contains Topeka, could provide an early read on the race; in 2024 it had mostly finished reporting its votes by 10 p.m. Eastern. Like Sedgwick, it was much bluer in the governor’s race: Kelly carried it by about 20 points, while Kamala Harris won it by less than one.

Josh Shapiro, a Democrat, easily won a second term as governor of Pennsylvania, defeating Stacy Garrity, the Republican state treasurer, The Associated Press reported. Given Shapiro’s broad favorability and huge fund-raising advantage, the outcome of the race was never in much doubt. This freed Shapiro to campaign for Democrats hoping to flip U.S. House seats in his crucial swing state, a gesture that could help his standing with Democrats nationwide should he decide to run for president in 2028.
A possible stunner may be brewing in the
South Carolina Senate race

, where Annie Andrews, the Democrat, has a narrow lead over Senator Darline Graham, the Republican, according to our estimates. While it’s still early, Andrews has done better than expected in the early vote, absentee vote and, crucially, in the first precincts to report on Election Day.

Gov. JB Pritzker of Illinois, a billionaire Democrat who is widely believed to be weighing a run for president, won a third term, The Associated Press reported. Pritzker prevailed in a rematch of his 2022 race with Darren Bailey, a Republican former state senator, in a solidly Democratic state. Pritzker has repeatedly sparred with President Trump, including when the president sought to deploy the military to Chicago during an immigration crackdown last year.
The Needle
is live
. It shows Democrats with a significant advantage in the House and an advantage in the Senate, based on returns from dozens of counties and precincts across the country.

content.text: In Dearborn, Mich., the city clerk, George Darany, said a precinct in the city was briefly out of ballots late in the day after workers there failed to alert the clerk’s office in time that it was running low. Five people waited as officials replenished the ballots within about 10 minutes. The clerk’s office also began delivering ballot applications, which were also running low in some places, to all precincts.

Mayor Abdullah Hammoud of Dearborn sent out an alert on social media about the ballot situation amid high turnout and long lines, and recommended that everyone stay in line to vote past the 8 p.m. closing time, if need be. “Let’s keep the momentum going, Dearborn. Every vote matters!” he wrote.

Earlier this evening, I was at a polling site in South Portland, Maine, where the Democratic nominee for Senate, Troy Jackson, stopped by to shake voters’ hands and deliver his closing argument to reporters. Jackson described himself as a “change agent” and argued that voters had had enough of the Republican incumbent, Senator Susan Collins.
We have our first competitive House race where most of the vote is counted:
Florida’s 13th Congressional District

, where Anna Paulina Luna, a Republican, leads by less than 0.2 points in a Trump +13 district with 95 percent of the vote counted. This race was rated “lean Republican” by the Cook Political Report, and it’s the first clear sign that Democrats are highly competitive in usually safely Republican districts.
Florida 13th Congressional District Election Results ›

Margins are expected to tighten in the Senate race in Georgia. Many of the metro Atlanta counties have reported results from early and mail-in ballots, which are leaning Democratic. But there are a lot of votes to come that are expected to benefit Mike Collins, the Republican nominee, including results from ballots cast on Election Day as well as from rural areas in the rest of the state.

The Democratic nominees for governor and Senate in Florida are very different types of Democrats, yet they are running close together so far. David Jolly, the nominee for governor, is a former Republican congressman who became a Democrat. Angie Nixon, the nominee for Senate, is a democratic socialist. Both are garnering roughly the same share of the vote so far.

The Senate race in Ohio, where polls just closed, was America’s most expensive general election this fall, clearing the $500 million mark in advertising spending. Republicans spent about 60 percent of the money used on the airwaves in that state, all part of an attempt to help the relatively little-known Republican incumbent, Senator Jon Husted. Some of that differential is attributable to the crypto industry. Husted was helped in the end by a crypto super PAC called Fairshake,
which spent over $46 million to try to oust Husted’s Democratic opponent, Sherrod Brown

Since 2008, just two Democrats have won a partisan statewide contest in Ohio: Sherrod Brown, who is back on the ballot this year after narrowly losing his bid for a fourth Senate term in 2024, and Barack Obama, who won the state twice before President Trump carried it by wide margins in each of his presidential campaigns.
Brown’s fortunes will partly hinge on a corridor of working-class counties in northern Ohio that backed both Obama and Trump, like
Mahoning
and
Portage

. Brown will also seek to cut into Senator Jon Husted’s margins in the Appalachian corner of the state that borders West Virginia. That was where he outperformed Kamala Harris the most in 2024. Keep an eye on
Delaware County
, too: Home to some of suburban Columbus, it’s a rare area in Ohio where Democrats have gained ground in recent years.

One worry that Republicans have had in Florida is that close statewide races — even if they are eventually won by Republicans — would mean stronger Democratic turnout in House races, possibly leading to surprises and upsets in a state where Republicans currently hold 20 out of 28 congressional seats.

The first vote drops in Florida were remarkably strong for Angie Nixon, the Democratic nominee for Senate, who was winning early votes in the majority-Hispanic counties of Miami-Dade and Osceola by 10 and 24 percentage points. Both of those counties had flipped to Republicans in 2024.

A rightward shift is likely to happen once Election Day votes start reporting in these counties, particularly because the partisan gap between Florida’s Election Day votes and early votes is smaller than it was two years ago.
Representative Anna Paulina Luna of Florida, a Republican congresswoman with celebrity status in MAGA circles,
appears to be locked in a tough fight
with Leela Gray, a retired Army brigadier general and a Democrat, in her St. Petersburg-based district.

Whatever happens tonight, the results will look very Democratic for the next half hour or longer — including in states where Democrats are considered underdogs, like Florida or South Carolina. That’s because most of these states report their early votes first, and the early vote was heavily Democratic this year. Republicans hope to counter with votes cast on Election Day, which will be reported later on.

President Trump appears to be watching Fox News, and he isn’t happy with what he’s seeing. The president has denounced the cable channel in three Truth Social posts within a span of 95 minutes, accusing the network of “spending too much time covering the Trump Deranged Dumocrats!” He added, at 7 p.m., that Fox News’s ratings were “way down, not because of me, but because they are AGAINST me!”

One contest to watch in Florida, where most polling places have begun to close, is the governor’s race. Florida has leaned Republican the last few elections. But life in the state has gotten very expensive, and that is one statewide race — between David Jolly, the Democrat, and Byron Donalds, the Republican — that both parties found to be much more competitive than they expected going into the midterms.

content.text: The incumbent Republican in Indiana’s Third Congressional District, Representative Marlin Stutzman, who is trailing with just 39 percent of votes reported, is a lawmaker who rarely makes waves or national headlines, but he gained attention this year when he
introduced a plan in Congress
to phase out direct military aid to Israel in favor of a transition to a joint defense and economic investment program between the country and the U.S.
The topic was thrust back into the news this morning when President Trump said that
direct military aid to Israel would be “cut off at the end of the year.”
Just before the polls closed, supporters of Angie Nixon, the Democratic candidate for Senate in Florida, made last-minute calls at her election-night watch party in Jacksonville to get out the vote.

At Ken Paxton’s watch party in Dallas, the campaign staff has wheeled out a cannon. It is unclear if the cannon is real or a replica. It resembles the famous cannon that became a symbol of the Battle of Gonzales in 1835, the first major military clash between settlers in what would eventually become Texas and the Mexican Army during the Texas Revolution. Paxton, a Republican, is running for the Senate against James Talarico, a Democrat seeking to win the first statewide race for his party since the 1990s.

President Trump is not expected to make a public appearance tonight, but he is sharing his real-time thoughts on Truth Social. So far, he is particularly angry about Fox News’s coverage tonight. An hour ago, Trump said he was turning off Fox because he “can’t stand Jessica Tarlov’s voice” and would return to the channel later. Tarlov is the resident liberal on Fox News. But Trump appears to still be watching Fox because he is now criticizing its polling. “Every question is a hit job,” he wrote.

The incumbent in Indiana’s Fifth Congressional District, Representative Victoria Spartz, is an idiosyncratic figure in the House G.O.P. conference and a frequent nuisance for Republican leaders. That is in part because of her reputation for changing her mind on how she plans to vote on major legislation at the last minute, including on the Republican budget bill teeing up her party’s marquee tax and spending cuts legislation.

House Democrats are watching three key races in Florida to provide them with some early signs of how the night is going: the re-election bids of Representatives Kathy Castor, Jared Moskowitz and Darren Soto. All are Democrats who are vulnerable this year because of Republican redistricting efforts, and their races are likely to be some of the early ones that are called tonight. If they win, Democrats said they expected more good news to follow through the night.

The first votes out of Indiana’s Fifth Congressional District show an advantage for Democrats. If reporting patterns are consistent with the 2024 presidential election, that first drop is early vote. In 2024, Kamala Harris won the first drop in Hamilton County, primarily consisting of early votes, by two percentage points, before ultimately losing the county by six. Tonight, J.D. Ford, the Democrat, is winning the first drop in Hamilton County by 27 points.
